questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I am torn between choosing acedemic opportunities or explore new cultures, because they were equally influential in my choiec to go abroad for a semester. I wanted new imput, and I wanted to experience how it is to attend university in another country. As much as I love UCPH I also craved different perspectives and ways to approach learning about my major.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: This exchange came at the perfect time for me, I gained so many awesome experiences, and I return with a renewed energy for mu studies and new eyes for my home city :')

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: That was pretty easy. We all received an email with all the information. It was a little delayed but it came and everything was fine.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The UCEAP office (education abroad program) was very helpful - I recommend contacting them if you have any questions.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I also called the UCEAP office with questions about my UCEAP application and got a hold of Paulette. She was so so helpful and she asisted me in bettering my application besides solving the technical issue I initially called her about.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There were multiple options for student housing that you can apply for through the university. You will most likely be sharing an apartment with a group of other students, and you will be living with little space. This is part of the experience and I really appreciated having people so near me to talk to and ask questions especially in the beginning. If you choose student housing over private owned I would recommend either San Joaquin Villages (this is where I lived), Sierra Madre or Santa Ynez (private owned apartments are often located closer to campus but they are also more expensive).

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: I didn't subscribe to a meal plan, but I know you can choose either a partly plan or a full plan where you can eat all your meals at the dining halls. I cooked all my food myself or ate out. The student housing kitchens are nice and well equipped, but it can feel a bit cramped when you and all your roommates are using it ( I lived with 6 other girls). Cleaning and decluttering is key!!

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer: That it will be sorted out eventually. I know people who hadn't succeeded in finding something before coming there, and they still found something really cool. If you don't get housing through the university, try facebook groups or simply just arrive in good time and look around. If you are into that kind of thing, there are some really cool co-ups in Isla Vista close to the UCSB campus where you live with and get to know many interesting people.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I really found the process of getting an overview of what courses they offered difficult and frustrating - I was so confused about where to look. I would recommend calling or writing the university directly with whatever questions you have. They are usually very responsive.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: After applying for a minimum of three of the UC campus locations (where you submit a study plan for each location) you receive your placement and get your host university. Then you have to enroll in your courses during your pass time. This happens after a first come firs serve principle, and I recommend you enlist as soon as possible. Many of the courses require an add code to enroll (especially if you choose outside your enlisted major) - you can get the add code by writing the professor teaching the course. It's a good idea to know which courses you want and to have collected the add codes for them before yur pass time opens.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I found emailing the professors directly very helpful.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I wanted, but this can be more difficult to achieve with other majors. I study psychology, and the prerequisites for this major overlaps with the prereqs for many other social sciences.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: As I wrote above: email the professors and enroll asap :)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I found the level of my courses somewhat alike to the level we have at home at UCPH. This was not the case for some of my friends in other majors, who found them way easier. I don't think I have heard about someone experiencing them as more difficult at UCSB than UCPH, but the UCSB certainly offered different perspectives that were fresh and interesting to me.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There are more test, assignments, and midterm exams throughout the quarter than we have at UCPH - this takes some of the weight off of the final exams, it seems more spread out. This can be a bit much, as you have to keep track of a lot of deadlines - but the assignments are usually small and I liked doing a bit all the time instead of a lot during finals week. Also, the quarters are super short (10 weeks) and there are no weeks without classes where you can revise material - this was new to me and a bit annoying, but we all managed, and it was not so bad.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Metaphilosophy (4 units, PHIL), Developmental Psychology (4 units, PSYCH), Cognitive Development (4 units, PSYCH), Health and Well Being (4 units, EDU), Organizing Difference (4 units, COMM), Corporate Social Responsibility (4 units, COMM), Global Ideologies and World Order (4 units, GLOBL)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Health and Well Being. I learned a lot and Professor Shism's teaching style was so engaging that we all got to know each other reall well.

questions.answer: The cost of groceries was higher than I expected. But we had a food bank on campus where you could pick up food for free, and that helped a lot. I recommend using that if you want to save money on groceries.

questions.answer: Look above

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: UCSB had so many cool on campus facilities. Pool, gym, climbing walls, soccer teams etc. If you like the outdoors I recommend you sign up with the Excursion Club which is a student driven club that organize trips hikes and random fun stuff - and they rent out gear you can use for surfing, SUP, camping and kayaking. It is awesome. Also check out shoreline for free fun activities organized by the university.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: So so many. I personnaly, joined a soccer team, attended free pilates classes every wednesday morning, went on trips with the excursion club - and I also recommend you go to some of the events in Campbell Hall - they have an Arts & Lectures programme, and students arrange a screening of The Rocky Horror Picture Show (must see).

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Look above :)

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I recommend you get together a group of frinds and borrow or rent a car and go places. California has so much to offer and road trips are awesome - these have been my favourite part of the exchange.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. People are very open and easy to talk to, and they are going to be curious about you and your home country, so the icebreaker is easy. And the chill vibe of a surfy campus by the beach is hard not to love.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: The excursion club!! This is a perfect place to meet friends. I paid only 60 bucks for being a member for the time I was there. Otherwise attend shoreline activities and try to talk to people. Also: Isla Vista occasionally offers band parties where local bands (often consisting of UCSB students) perform - and they are really really good. You can follow the instagram @soundsofiv where they post about when and where the concerts will take place. Once or twice a year they move the band party to a location in the mountains, and that is a magical experience.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: This is really not a thing I struggled with a lot.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Their openness. Californians are not shy, and you can easily have a full blown conversation with a complete stranger.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Enjoy your time there before it runs out
2. Join Excursion Club and go camping
3. Go watch the sunset at Sands Beach

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: They have awesome thrift stores in Goleta. Old Town Coffee in Goleta is a nice café. Apna in Santa Barbara Downtown is a nice Indian place. You must go check out The Funk Zone in Santa Barbara Downtown if you like a chill and cozy night life more than clubbing (there is also super nice here during the day).

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people I met and the places I saw <3

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The time difference and missing my family friend, and boyfriend at home. But it is manageable if you plan your calls :)

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
